USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed now with a targeted Section 301 tariff package sized to the estimated annual harm from China's forced technology transfer and IP practices (on the order of $30 billion of Chinese imports, not an open-ended cascade), aimed at Made in China 2025 / tech-adjacent goods rather than consumer staples. Pair the tariff signal with a standing offer to negotiate structural IP, JV, and licensing changes, and do not stack another global 232-style measure that further isolates allies. Leave investment-screening and a WTO track as complementary tools, but make the immediate action a calibrated tariff so Beijing faces a concrete cost for the practices that survived the November 2017 Beijing visit.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a mild US opportunity, not a high or existential hit. The US macro backdrop as of mid-March 2018 is still expansionary: Michigan sentiment at 101.4, industrial production rising to 102.2, and no crisis-level stress (VIX ~17.9 after the February spike). The goods deficit remains large (BOPGTB about -$70bn) and imports from China are still the leverage point (~$38bn in the latest month; 2017 Chinese goods imports were cited above $500bn). China's economy is not distressed either (industrial output still ~6% y/y, reserves ~$3.16tn, CNY stronger near 6.32), so this is not a panic-driven moment. The underlying commercial injury is real and unremedied: the August 2017 Section 301 investigation targeted forced tech transfer, discriminatory licensing, state-directed acquisitions, and cyber-enabled IP theft; the November 2017 Beijing trip produced commercial MOUs but no structural IP concessions. That is why the threat reading is negative (opportunity/leverage) rather than zero: the US has unused, legitimate pressure on an issue with broader domestic buy-in than steel/aluminum. Action is moderate escalation, not maximal, because second-order risks are already visible. Section 232 steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) proclamations of 1–8 March are global, China is a small direct metals supplier, and Beijing has been cautious on 232 while warning that a China-specific follow-on will draw a justified and necessary response, with soybeans, aircraft, coal, and other politically resonant exports already named. More than half of US soybean exports go to China; farm groups and a 44-organization business coalition (Chamber, ITI and others) have warned that sweeping tariffs would invite retaliation and raise US costs. Lighthizer told Congress on 21 March that a 301 announcement was imminent and officials had framed ~$30bn as the annual forced-transfer cost, with the President asking for a larger figure — that is the right instrument and roughly the right scale, not a $100bn opening salvo or a concession. Holding or rolling back would ratify the post-Beijing status quo; going maximal would turn a leverage opportunity into a farm-belt and ally-cohesion problem before talks have even been tested against a real tariff. Intended numeric stance: threat about minus zero point three (mild opportunity); action about minus zero point four five (moderate tariff escalation).
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer case completed in substance; Beijing visit produced no structural concessions
US economy still strong (sentiment, IP, no crisis vol) so limited tariffs are absorbable
Large bilateral goods imbalance is US leverage; China not in FX/reserve distress
232 metals tariffs already strained allies and are a weak China-specific tool
Credible China retaliation path through soybeans, aircraft, and other politically sensitive US exports
Business/farm coalition opposition argues for a targeted $30bn-scale package, not a cascade

Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump announces plan to impose 25% tariff on steel and 10% on aluminum imports (Section 232). Global scope; China is a smaller direct supplier share than some other exporters.
Trump signs Section 232 proclamations imposing the steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) tariffs.
US consumer sentiment 101.4 as of 2018-03-01, still elevated.
US industrial production 102.2067 (2017=100) in March 2018, up over the window.
US goods trade balance still deeply negative at -$69,809 million (2018-03).
CNY at 6.32 per USD on 2018-03-21, stronger vs ~6.62 in late Sept 2017; no China FX-stress signal.
China reserves excluding gold about $3.16 trillion in March 2018, stable to slightly higher.
Lighthizer told Ways and Means a 301 announcement was imminent; ~$30bn tariffs expected; China signaled it would not hide from a fight; soybeans and airplanes named as likely retaliation targets.
Lighthizer presented a $30bn 301 package equal to estimated annual forced-transfer cost; Trump asked for a larger number; investment restrictions still being legally scrubbed.
Administration to propose tariffs on at least $30bn of Chinese imports; 44 business groups warned sweeping tariffs would provoke retaliation and raise US costs.
Wang Yi: trade wars are never the solution; China will make a justified and necessary response; CISA urged hits on US agriculture, coal, electronics.
More than half of US soybean exports go to China; Midwest farmers and ASA warned Brazil/Argentina can replace US beans.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Answer the already-signed Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs with a calibrated, WTO-framed retaliation on politically sensitive U.S. exports (continue and, if needed, expand the sorghum anti-dumping track; prepare a short, targeted agricultural list) while keeping a live channel for talks on the still-unannounced Section 301 package. Do not concede Made in China 2025 / tech-transfer architecture, and do not launch a broad pre-emptive tariff war before USTR actually publishes findings and remedies. The aim is deterrence and domestic credibility after the Liu He snub, not a race to the bottom.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not yet high. The live U.S. measures as of 21 March are Section 201 solar/washer safeguards (22 Jan) and global Section 232 metals tariffs signed 8 March; China is a small direct steel supplier (~2% of U.S. steel imports), so the realized export hit is limited. The larger danger is prospective: a 300-page Section 301 report and shock-value tariff/investment package aimed at IP, forced tech transfer, and industrial policy is expected imminently (Politico, 21 Mar; Trump 7 Mar tweet; Covington 15 Mar). That targets the development model, not just metals. Macro data do not yet show a bite: industrial production still ~6% y/y, reserves ~$3.16tn and stable, discount rate unchanged at 2.9%, and CNY stronger (~6.32 vs ~6.62 six months earlier), so this is not FX stress or export-hub unemployment. Action should therefore be a measured mirror of 232, not maximal escalation and not concession. Beijing has already vowed “necessary measures” and opened a sorghum AD probe after the January safeguards; U.S. soy (~$12bn) is the obvious larger lever and is already spooking the farm belt, but a full soy cutoff would also raise Chinese feed/pork costs. Unilateral U.S. 232 and “trade wars are good, and easy to win” have irritated third parties, so China can retaliate proportionally, file at the WTO, and still invite negotiation on 301 without pre-paying structural reform.
key_factors: Section 301 findings and remedies are imminent but not yet published; the live fight is still 201/232
232 metals tariffs are signed but China’s direct steel/aluminum exposure is small
China macro still healthy: IP ~+6% y/y, reserves stable, CNY firmer — dispute not biting the real economy
U.S. farm-belt (sorghum already probed; soy the larger lever) is the highest-leverage, lowest-self-harm retaliation channel if kept calibrated
Liu He talks were undercut by the 232 announcement; some visible response is needed for credibility without locking in a larger 301 package
U.S. unilateralism and ally irritation create space to frame China as defending multilateral rules

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit).
Trump announces plan to impose 25% tariff on steel and 10% on aluminum imports (Section 232). Global scope; China is a smaller direct supplier share than some other exporters.
Trump tweets: "trade wars are good, and easy to win."
Trump signs Section 232 proclamations imposing the steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) tariffs.
China industrial production still ~106.0 (same period previous year = 100) as of 2018-03; growth intact, not a recessionary export shock.
China total reserves ex-gold ~$3.16tn in March 2018, slightly higher over the window — no reserve-drain / financial-stability stress.
CNY/USD ~6.32 on 21 Mar 2018 versus ~6.62 in late Sep 2017 (yuan stronger, not under tariff-driven depreciation pressure).
Expected ~300-page Section 301 report with recommendations; tariff action described as geared more toward shock value and leverage than methodical engagement.
More worrying to China are separate Section 301 sanctions; hundreds of Chinese companies could be singled out.
China is only a little more than 2% of U.S. steel imports; Beijing’s initial 232 reaction was cautious and still hoped to keep talking.
MOFCOM “resolutely opposed” 232 and said China will assess damage and firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.
China already launched a sorghum AD probe after January safeguards; soybeans (over half of U.S. soy exports) are the widely discussed next lever.
After 232, U.S. is poised to implement 301 sanctions on China IP; Beijing has signaled it is prepared to respond, including via politically sensitive tariffs and WTO challenge.
